## Now you know which parts you kept rewriting

By the end of a capstone, a handful of things have started recurring: event
playback, bar validation, transposition, chord voicing, articulation, source
reporting. Repetition is evidence for a library, and it's only evidence once the
helper's inputs and behaviour have settled. Extract too early and you promote a
provisional decision into an API that everything afterwards has to work around.

Finish at least one of Lessons 55, 56 or 57 before you start this. A finished
project hands you real call sites, awkward events and provenance fields to judge
an abstraction against. Without those, a library design mostly records your
expectations about music you haven't represented yet.

Pick one event schema and stay with it. `:note`, `:start` and `:duration` have
been the centre since Part 3, with `:amp` present when dynamics belong to score
data. Migrate older pieces onto that schema; the alternative is teaching every helper
to accept `:duration`, `:dur` and `:length`. A compatibility branch buys you
convenience today and installs permanent ambiguity in everything you write
afterwards.

Keep the framework small enough that a score stays readable. A helper should
remove repeated machinery and leave the musical decisions visible at the call
site. If you can't see what the music does without opening two functions, the
abstraction has taken something it shouldn't have.

## A candidate library, and the theme it started from

The theme below is the phrase from the setup buffer, the one you ran before
[Lesson 1](../00-getting-a-sound-out/01-hello-sound.qmd) existed for you. It now carries dynamics, absolute starts, and a
validator that will refuse it if any of that is malformed.

```{.ruby audio=""}
use_bpm 78

define :validate_events do |events, expected_end|
  raise "empty score" if events.empty?

  events.each do |event|
    required = [:note, :start, :duration]
    missing = required.reject { |key| event.key?(key) }
    raise "missing keys: #{missing}" unless missing.empty?
    raise "duration must be positive" unless event[:duration] > 0
  end

  actual_end = events.map { |event| event[:start] + event[:duration] }.max
  raise "expected end #{expected_end}, got #{actual_end}" unless actual_end == expected_end
end

define :transpose_events do |events, semitones|
  events.map do |event|
    event.merge(note: note(event[:note]) + semitones)
  end
end

define :play_events do |events, synth_name|
  use_synth synth_name
  cursor = 0.0
  events.each do |event|
    sleep event[:start] - cursor
    play event[:note],
      release: event[:duration] * 0.82,
      amp: event.fetch(:amp, 0.8)
    cursor = event[:start]
  end
  sleep events.last[:duration]
end

# The phrase from setup.qmd, with dynamics and absolute starts.
theme = [
  {note: :e4, start: 0.0, duration: 1.0, amp: 0.62},
  {note: :g4, start: 1.0, duration: 1.0, amp: 0.68},
  {note: :a4, start: 2.0, duration: 1.0, amp: 0.72},
  {note: :b4, start: 3.0, duration: 1.0, amp: 0.78},
  {note: :d5, start: 4.0, duration: 2.0, amp: 0.88},
  {note: :b4, start: 6.0, duration: 1.0, amp: 0.74},
  {note: :g4, start: 7.0, duration: 1.0, amp: 0.62}
]

validate_events theme, 8.0
play_events theme, :piano
sleep 1
play_events transpose_events(theme, 7), :pluck
```

Three helpers, one score. Validation, transposition and rendering all take the
same event shape, so they compose without adapters and without a second copy of
the data. `transpose_events` returns new hashes via `merge` and never mutates
the original, which is why you can play the theme again afterwards and get the
theme.

Notice what `play_events` doesn't do. It doesn't validate, it doesn't transpose,
and it has no opinion about bars. Every one of those was a separate lesson, and
keeping them separate is what lets you replace any one of them.

## Three ways to test whether the boundary holds

1. Delete `:duration` from any event and run it. The validator names the missing
   key and stops before a note sounds. Now delete the `validate_events` call
   instead and run the same broken score. What breaks, and how far from the
   actual mistake does the failure surface?
2. Change the release ratio in `play_events` from `0.82` to `1.1`. Every note
   now overruns its neighbour. The score is untouched, and articulation was
   never in it.
3. Call `transpose_events(theme, 7)` twice in a row and play the result. Fourteen
   semitones up, and the theme survives intact because the function is pure. Try
   writing a mutating version and running it twice to see what you'd have lost.

## What belongs in a library and what doesn't

A helper earns its place by removing machinery, not by hiding decisions.
`play_events` removes cursor arithmetic you'd otherwise retype in every buffer,
and it leaves pitch, timing and dynamics fully visible in the score. Compare
that with a hypothetical `play_nice_melody(theme)` that picks a synth, a release
ratio and a swing amount for you. It would be shorter to call and it would put
the musical decisions somewhere you can no longer see them.

The schema is where the real leverage is. Because every helper agrees on
`:note`, `:start` and `:duration`, they compose in any order:
`play_events(transpose_events(theme, 7), :pluck)` needs no glue. Introduce a
second event shape and you'll need a converter at every boundary between them,
and converters are where the errors go to live.

Write the README for whoever opens this in a year, remembering Ruby and nothing
else. They'll need to know why starts are absolute rather than sequential, how
you represent a rest, and which layer controls articulation. Those three
questions are exactly the ones that are expensive to answer by reading the code,
because in each case the answer is a decision rather than a mechanism.

Absolute starts, to take the first one, cost more to type and buy you a
timeline where one bad duration leaves every later coordinate alone. That
trade-off was worth making for transcription work in Part 9. Someone building
generative loops might reasonably decide the other way. A README that records
the reason lets a future reader disagree with you deliberately.

## Where this leaves you

Fifty-eight lessons ago, that theme was eight symbols and a `sleep`. It now
carries dynamics, validated structure, absolute time, and a rendering layer that
can be swapped without touching a note. Nothing was added to the music. What
grew was the representation, and it grew because each lesson asked it a question
the previous version couldn't answer.

That's the whole argument of the book, and you can check it yourself: open
`setup.qmd`, look at the array, and look at the score above. Same eight pitches.

The parts that remain are the ones a program can't settle. Whether your
transcription matches the recording, whether the shaped performance is
convincing, whether an octave leap is an error or the best thing in the line.
Those need your ears, and the tooling exists to get you to those questions
faster, with fewer routine mistakes in the way.

## Build the library, then justify it

Extract your recurring helpers into one file with a single event schema, and
migrate at least one earlier piece onto it. Write the README, and make it answer
those three questions: why absolute starts, how rests are represented, which
layer owns articulation.

Then do the part that's easy to skip. For each helper, write one sentence naming
the decision it does *not* make. If you can't name one, that helper is deciding
something on your behalf, and you should find out what before it decides it
again in a piece you care about.
